variants.headline: {{cityName}} completes the {{building}}
body: The last scaffold plank came down from the {{building}} in {{cityName}} on Tuesday, and the street outside has been full ever since. Masons washed the dust off their hands and went home, and the keeper has already asked for a second set of keys. The doors open to the public this week.

variants.headline: Notice from {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is ready
body: To all who have business at the {{building}}: the work at {{cityName}} is finished, and the doors stand open from this week. The keeper asks visitors to come by daylight while the lamps are being fitted.

variants.headline: Now fix the gutter
body: By the time the {{building}} in {{cityName}} was done, every mason had a story about it. The best belongs to the boy who carried water: he sat on the finished roof with his legs over the edge and would not come down until his mother promised him a place at the opening. Below, she said the gutter could wait until Monday.

variants.headline: Another job for the builders of {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has its {{building}} and a work crew that knows every gate and stair of it. The foreman has kept the whole gang on the books, which costs money every week the tools sit idle. If the {{terms.civic.government}} has a second project drawn up, this is the month to hand it over.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} puts money behind the {{building}}
body: Fresh scaffolding went up around the {{building}} at {{cityName}} this week, and the gate guards have stopped counting the carts. The city has put more money into the job, and the crew now works two shifts. Neighbors who had given up on the site are bringing chairs out to watch it rise.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} funds the {{building}}
body: Word from {{cityName}}: the {{building}} has received a fresh sum from the city chest, and the work will not pause for want of wages. The stewards will publish the accounts at the site each week.

variants.headline: Why {{cityName}} is paying for the {{building}}
body: Money put into the {{building}} at {{cityName}} bought one thing above all: a shorter wait. The scaffold holds more hands than it did a month ago, and the keeper has been given a date to open. The cost sits in the city chest, where other works will feel it, and only the finished building can answer whether the trade was fair.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Coin speeds the {{building}}
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! The city has put its coin behind the {{building}}, and the hammers do not stop at sundown! Lamps on the scaffold, carts on the road, and the roof going up while the rest of us sleep!

variants.headline: {{cityName}} buys the {{building}}
body: The {{building}} in {{cityName}} opened this morning without a single plank left in the street. The city paid in {{currency}} and took delivery of the finished work, and a line had formed at the door before the shutters were fully open.

variants.headline: No wait in {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is bought
body: Most towns wait years for a {{building}}, and watch the brick go up one course at a time. {{cityName}} skipped all that: the city counted out {{currency}}, and the doors opened the same season. The masons who would have built it are still looking for work.

variants.headline: A purchase for {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is ready
body: Notice is given that {{cityName}} now holds its {{building}}, secured with {{currency}} and open to use. The bargain was struck and settled in one season, which is quicker than raising the thing stone by stone, and the city enjoys it from this day.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} pays for speed
body: At {{cityName}} the {{building}} arrived without a building season: the city handed over {{currency}} and took the keys the same week. What the purchase bought was time, and the price is set down in the city's accounts. Whether the hurry was worth it depends on what else the same price might have done, and no ledger records what was never tried.

variants.headline: {{largest}} outgrows the capital
body: The census clerk in {{largest}} ran out of room on his tally sheet this week and sent a boy for another. The city now counts {{largestPopulation}} people, more than {{capital}} can claim. The largest crowd in the realm now gathers somewhere other than the capital.

variants.headline: {{largest}} pass the capital
body: The tally is level at the top: {{largest}} each hold {{largestPopulation}} people, and each has passed {{capital}}. A mapmaker in the capital has been redrawing the city marks to scale, and the towns on his table now come out wider than the one under his window.

variants.headline: {{largest}} now outweighs {{capital}}
body: By the latest count, {{largest}} has more people than {{capital}}. Power has not moved with them: the {{terms.civic.government}} still sits in the capital, and the petitions still travel there. In {{largest}}, the clerk who bundles those petitions has asked for a larger mail sack, which may be the quietest way a capital learns it has a rival.

variants.headline: {{capital}} loses its crown to {{largest}}
body: The orators at the corner of the {{capital}} square have dropped their oldest line, the one about the biggest city in the realm. {{largest}} counts {{largestPopulation}} people now, and the crowds have followed the numbers. They still draw a hearing, just not the largest one.

variants.headline: The capital just got outgrown
body: {{largest}} now counts more residents than {{capital}}, {{largestPopulation}} at the last count. The {{terms.civic.government}} still meets in the capital. The crowds do not.

variants.headline: The same grievance in {{count|city|cities}}
body: Town clerks in {{count}} of our cities have written the same word at the top of their complaint books: {{key}}. A grievance that turns up in that many places at once has stopped being a local matter, and the capital will have to answer it as one.

variants.headline: One problem, {{count|city|cities}}
body: When the same complaint leads in {{count}} of our cities, the cause is {{key}}, and it has become policy whether or not anyone wrote it down. Bad weather explains one bad season in one town. This many towns, all with the same grievance, points to a decision made in the capital and never revisited by the {{terms.civic.government}}.

variants.headline: Hunger in {{count}} of our cities
body: {{count}} of our cities now put hunger at the top of the list. Anyone standing in a bread line could have told you that months ago.

variants.headline: Boredom in {{count|city|cities}}
body: {{count}} of our cities have the same complaint: nothing to do after the day's work. The squares empty early, the benches go unused, and the same three songs carry the whole evening.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is being razed
body: {{civilization}} has set {{cityName}} ablaze, and the fire is being fed on purpose. Unless something changes, {{turns}} more will leave nothing on the site but ash and the roads that led to it.

variants.headline: A city held by {{civilization}} is being razed
body: Smoke from a burning city held by {{civilization}} can be seen from the border road. Its name has not reached us, but the fire will have {{turns}} more before the site is bare.

variants.headline: {{population}} people remain as {{cityName}} is razed
body: {{population}} people are still inside {{cityName}} while {{civilization}} burns it. No order has come to stop the fire, and the fire has {{turns}} more at the present pace. Families at the north gate have begun stacking their belongings by the road, ready to move the moment the gate opens.

variants.headline: A city burns {{distance}} from our nearest city
body: Word has come from the frontier that {{civilization}} is burning {{cityName}}, {{distance}} from the nearest of our towns. Travelers from that road speak of smoke lying flat over the fields at midday. This office will print the next dispatch the moment a rider brings one.

variants.headline: The end of {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has only {{turns}} left. Then its walls, its market and its shrines will be gone together, by the will of {{civilization}}. The prayers said there will not stop, but they will be said under another roof, and nothing will remain to show who knelt.

variants.headline: Flags change over {{cityName}}
body: The same city has changed hands more than once, and each report has been printed as it came. {{merge.values.transfers}}{{merge.values.holder}} Its people have learned to wait before repainting the gate.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is ours
body: {{cityName}} is ours, taken from {{formerOwner}} by force of arms. Our flag went up over the gate before the dust settled, and the city's walls, its granaries and its people passed with it.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is ours
body: {{cityName}} has fallen to our troops. The dispatches do not name the power that held it, only that its flag came down and ours went up.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{captor}}
body: {{captor}} has wrested {{cityName}} from us. The gates are in their hands, the garrison is broken, and the people who cheered our flag last season now answer to another.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is lost
body: {{cityName}} no longer answers to us. No report names the power that took it, and no messenger has come through with terms; the loss is certain even where the details are not.

variants.headline: A city changes hands
body: A city has changed hands, and ours were the hands on one side of it. No dispatch names the place or the power, but somewhere a gate opened this morning to soldiers who were not there yesterday. The clerks will have the name soon enough; the families inside already know it.

variants.headline: What {{cityName}} adds
body: {{cityName}} is ours, and with it the roads, the wells and the high ground around it. The gain brings people and workshops, but it also brings a wall to man and a population that has not yet decided to be loyal. Armies take cities in an afternoon; holding one is a longer campaign.

variants.headline: Who is taking names for {{cityName}}?
body: The afternoon {{cityName}} fell, a laundress on our street began asking carters what it would cost to carry a letter across the new border. Three of them named a price and none would promise delivery. Councilors, open a desk where families may leave letters, and use the road you found so quickly when there were taxes to collect.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} finishes new defenses
body: {{cityName}} has a finished {{building}}, and the gatekeeper has spent the morning testing its new fittings. Masons are still clearing rubble from the ditch, but the wall behind them could turn back a raid today.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} strengthens its walls
body: Sentries at {{cityName}} have moved their posts to the new height, now that the {{building}} is done. The officer of the watch says an attacking column would need ladders it did not bring.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is ready for a siege
body: {{cityName}}, hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! The {{building}} is done, stone on stone, and the watch has climbed into it! Sleep easier tonight, and let the enemy count our walls from the road!

variants.headline: A stronger {{cityName}}
body: It is confirmed that the {{building}} at {{cityName}} is complete. The {{terms.civic.government}} ordered the work before the danger was plain, and the watch is now installed there. Visitors will find the gate open at the usual hours.

variants.headline: Famine grips {{city}}
body: The bakeries of {{city}} shut their shutters before noon now, and the queues form an hour earlier each week. Hunger has become the city's loudest grievance, counted at {{famine}} of its discontent. The market square empties as soon as the bread is gone.

variants.headline: Why {{city}} is hungry
body: A city that cannot feed itself has one question to answer, and {{city}} has not answered it. Famine accounts for {{famine}} of the city's discontent, the biggest share of its troubles. The granaries did not empty by themselves, and the men who count the harvest owe the city an explanation.

variants.headline: Empty stalls in {{city}}
body: The bread cart in {{city}} used to come at eight and leave at ten. Now it arrives at seven and is empty before the morning bell. The driver has stopped apologizing; he just turns the horse around and lets the crowd see the empty bed.

variants.headline: A call for bread in {{city}}
body: The faithful of {{city}} are asked to bring what they can spare to the shrine steps. Famine outweighs every other burden in the city, and the stores must last until the next harvest. A loaf given away today is a prayer answered tomorrow.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} changes allegiance
body: {{cityName}} has thrown off {{formerOwner}} and declared for {{newOwner}}. The change came by revolt, not by treaty, and the town hall spent the morning stamping new seals on old papers.

variants.headline: Old orders under a new flag in {{cityName}}
body: After a season of unrest, {{cityName}} has left {{formerOwner}} for {{newOwner}}. The city's markets sit where two customs systems meet, and every merchant with goods in transit is now guessing which duty applies. The first wagon held at the gate will tell the city more about its new rulers than any proclamation.

variants.headline: Madam, we are {{newOwner}} now
body: Madam, the flag over our square has changed, and the clerks have already rewritten the headings on every form. We who live in {{cityName}} did not move: the same bakers, the same boatmen, the same children in the lane. {{newOwner}} inherits our trade and our taxes; we ask that the first be encouraged and the second be gentle. The quarrel with {{formerOwner}} was never ours.

variants.headline: The flag changed overnight in {{cityName}}
body: The watchman on the east gate of {{cityName}} changed flags at dawn, then went home and slept through the arguing. By noon the square had two crowds, one cheering {{newOwner}} and one muttering about {{formerOwner}}, and the same baker was selling bread to both.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} reaches {{population}} people
body: The newest lane in {{cityName}} already has washing lines across it. With {{population}} people counted, the city has become a {{milestone}}, and the council has begun arguing about where the next well should go.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} crosses {{population}}
body: {{cityName}} has crossed into {{milestone}} territory at {{population}} people, a line that changes what the city can ask of the realm. Its market now runs past the afternoon bell, and the potters have fired a second kiln to keep up. More people mean more hands, more trade and louder demands on the roads and wells, and a city that meets those demands will not stay at this size for long.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} has grown to {{population}}!
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! {{cityName}} now counts {{population}} souls and has earned the name of {{milestone}}! Count the chimneys, count the carts, and say the word aloud: {{milestone}}!

variants.headline: A milestone for {{cityName}}
body: We are informed that {{cityName}} has reached {{population}} people and is now reckoned a {{milestone}}. The older families will tell you that the well queue has grown and the walk to it has lengthened. Growth of this kind comes slowly, and the city is the better for having waited for it.

variants.headline: {{liberator}} liberates {{liberated}}
body: The flag of {{liberated}} went up over its own square at first light, after {{liberator}} drove out the occupiers. Crowds filled the square before the ropes were secured, and the old anthem was sung badly and repeatedly.

variants.headline: Our independence is restored
body: Our long occupation is over. {{liberator}} has restored the nation to its own government, and the council chamber that answered to a foreign governor now answers to us. The guard outside it wears our colors again.

variants.headline: {{liberated}} is free again
body: {{liberated}} is free again, by our own soldiers' hands. The nation that had lived under another's banner raised its own this week, and its council has taken up the business of governing itself.

variants.headline: A nation restored: {{liberated}} is free
body: Letters from {{liberated}} relate that the nation has resumed its independence, restored by the arms of {{liberator}}. At its council hall, the old seal was broken and a new one cut, and the first act of the returned government was to send thanks.

variants.headline: Freedom for {{liberated}}
body: {{liberated}} flies its own flag again, and {{liberator}} made that possible. A nation restored is a friend for a generation; a nation annexed is a wound that never closes. Let this paper's readers remember which of the two {{liberator}} chose.

variants.headline: Pillaged land weighs on {{city}}
body: The fields south of {{city}} still show the raiders' tracks, and the farmsteads along the road stand empty. Pillage is now the city's heaviest burden, set down at {{pillaged}} in its own accounts. Nothing has been rebuilt since the last raid.

variants.headline: The fields around {{city}} lie in ruin
body: The land around {{city}} was stripped, and the city's own count of its discontent puts pillage at {{pillaged}}, the heaviest entry. Raiders do the damage in a night; rebuilding it takes seasons, seed and hands. The men who decide where the garrison is posted should be asked why the fields were left unguarded.

variants.headline: The road to {{city}} is empty now
body: On the road south of {{city}}, the cart track that once carried vegetables to market now carries only dust. The farms beyond it stand stripped, and the families who worked them have gone to live with relatives inside the walls. The city names pillage as its heaviest complaint, and the empty road agrees.

variants.headline: {{city}} counts the cost of pillage
body: The city of {{city}} reports {{pillaged}} of its discontent owing to pillaged land, the largest single cause. The damage lies outside the walls, beyond the city's own reach. Towns that can spare wagons, seed or labor are asked to send word to the council.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} holds with damaged defenses
body: {{cityName}} still stands, though its walls are badly broken. Families living near the rampart have moved their bedding to relatives deeper inside, and the market has been moved into the shadow of the keep.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} holds against the siege
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}} of {{cityName}}! The enemy is at the gate, and the wall holds, sound to {{hitPoints}} of its {{maxHitPoints|stone|stones}}! Bring water to the rampart and keep the fires low! The wall holds! The wall holds!

variants.headline: Can {{cityName}} repair its walls under siege?
body: The question in {{cityName}} is not whether the wall will hold this week but whether it can be mended at all. Masons need stone, and stone comes by road, and the road is the first thing a besieging army takes. Every day the garrison spends without an attack is a day it should be hauling and mixing, not resting.

variants.headline: Life inside besieged {{cityName}}
body: Inside {{cityName}}, the shopkeepers have taken to trading behind half-closed shutters. Prices are chalked fresh each morning, and nobody argues about them. At night the whole city listens to the same sound, the creak of the gate and the men on the wall above it.

variants.headline: The defense of {{cityName}} continues
body: We are advised that {{cityName}} remains under siege, its wall sound to {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints|stone|stones}}. The watch changes without a gap, and the commanders report stores sufficient. Citizens are asked to keep the streets clear for runners.

variants.headline: A new colony {{distance}} from the capital
body: Our settlers have raised {{cityName}}, {{distance}} out from the capital. The first night's fires were still burning when the headman began assigning plots. Whatever the town becomes, it will owe that first winter to nobody but itself.

variants.headline: A colony far from the capital
body: A new settlement now stands {{distance}} beyond the capital. Its name has not been entered in our records, and no official has yet been sent to give it one.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is a long way from home
body: {{cityName}} sits {{distance}} from the capital, which is an outpost however the map is drawn. Every wagon of grain and every order from the capital will travel that distance, and so will any army sent to defend it. Yet a town that far out will pull a road after it, and roads draw settlers and trade behind them.

variants.headline: A new town, {{distance}} out
body: Word has come of a town called {{cityName}}, planted {{distance}} out from home. Its settlers are brave or desperate, and probably both. This paper wishes them well and notes who will be asked to pay for the road out to them.

variants.headline: A colony at {{cityName}}
body: Advice reaches us of {{cityName}}, newly founded {{distance}} from the capital. The settlement begins with a cleared site, a few stores and the labor of its own people. Traders wishing to reach it should ask the market office for the route.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} completes the {{building}} in {{cityName}}
body: From our hillside we watched the last scaffold come down at {{cityName}}. The {{building}} is finished, and {{civilization}} wasted no time filling it. The road to the city is carrying carts again.

variants.headline: New work near our border
body: {{civilization}} has finished a {{building}} in one of the cities along our border. The place has no name in our reports, but the work is close enough to be counted from our side.

variants.headline: New works at {{cityName}}
body: A new {{building}} stands finished at {{cityName}}, and {{civilization}} did not build it for our convenience. Works of this kind change what a neighbor can do on this frontier, and the change is already in place. Our own plans should be made on the assumption that the next one is already under way.

variants.headline: From beyond our border: {{cityName}} completes the {{building}}
body: Word arrives from across the border that {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}, has completed its {{building}}. Our watchers report the road busy all season and quiet since the roof went on. Traders bound that way should expect a quiet road for some days yet.

variants.headline: A neighbor's new work
body: Travelers coming through {{cityName}} all describe the same thing: the {{building}} standing open with no scaffold in sight. Nobody in the market could say when the work had begun, and the builders seem to have preferred it that way.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} buys the {{building}} in {{cityName}}
body: Scaffolding never went up at the {{building}} in {{cityName}}. {{civilization}} paid in {{currency}} for the finished work, and the first people through the door found the mortar still damp.

variants.headline: A purchase near our border
body: {{civilization}} has bought a {{building}} outright in a city near our border. No report gives its name. The sum was paid in {{currency}}, and the work changed hands finished.

variants.headline: {{civilization}} pays for the {{building}} near our border
body: At {{cityName}} the {{building}} was bought, not built: {{civilization}} paid and took it finished. A neighbor that buys its works outright has means to spare and a reason to want them sooner. Both are worth counting.

variants.headline: A neighbor's deep purse
body: Traders from {{cityName}} tell it as a joke: one month a fenced pit, the next a finished {{building}} with its door open. {{civilization}} paid in {{currency}} and skipped the years of dust. The joke is funnier in our market than in theirs.

variants.headline: Notice from {{cityName}}: the {{building}} is bought
body: It is learned that {{civilization}} has bought the {{building}} at {{cityName}}, the account settled in {{currency}}. The work passed complete into their hands, and the city has the use of it without the delay of building.

variants.headline: A new town on the doorstep of {{ours}}
body: {{player}} has planted {{city}} {{distance}} from {{ours}}, close enough that a farmer can see the new roofs from his field. No boundary has been surveyed between the two, and both towns will want the same spring.

variants.headline: A rival town rises close to home
body: {{player}} has founded a town {{distance}} from one of our cities. The ground between them, open last season, now has a rival's fences across it.

variants.headline: {{player}} plants a town near {{ours}}
body: {{city}} sits {{distance}} off {{ours}}, near enough that our farmers and theirs will be arguing over the same ground before the season is out. {{player}} calls it a settlement; a soldier would call it a post, and it is placed where a post does the most good for them. The next move on this border will be ours, and it will be judged by how quickly it comes.

variants.headline: {{city}} rises beside {{ours}}
body: {{player}} has put a town called {{city}} {{distance}} from {{ours}}, and the fields our families have worked for generations are now a frontier. Nothing about this is settled by a map drawn far away. Survey the line, plant the stones and tell the farmers where it runs, or the first harvest dispute will be settled by whoever is standing in the field.

variants.headline: New neighbors at {{city}}
body: We learn that {{player}} has founded {{city}}, {{distance}} from {{ours}}. A border this close will test the patience of both peoples, and it will also put a new market within a morning's ride of our merchants. Trade is the cheapest way to keep a neighbor friendly.

variants.headline: {{city}} comes under direct rule
body: The flag over {{city}} has not moved, but the men who give its orders now ride from {{owner}} itself. The city's years as a puppet are over, and its taxes go straight into the treasury that governs it.

variants.headline: {{owner}} tightens its hold on {{city}}
body: {{city}} was a puppet last season and is a province now, ruled directly from {{owner}}. The city lies {{distance}} from our own, which puts a tighter, more responsive government on our doorstep. Provinces obey faster than puppets, and that difference will show up on this border first.

variants.headline: A puppet no more: {{city}} answers to {{owner}}
body: {{owner}} has taken {{city}} under direct rule, and the change is more than paperwork. A puppet bargains; a province is told what to send. The men and grain of {{city}} are now at {{owner}}'s call without the delay of local consent.

variants.headline: A change of rule in {{city}}
body: Notice is given of a change in {{city}}: the city, lately a puppet, now answers to {{owner}} directly. The ceremonies were brief and the garrison unchanged. What has changed is who may issue orders and how fast they travel.

variants.headline: Resistance continues in {{cityName}}
body: The clerks in {{cityName}} write their orders twice now, once to send and once to file away when nothing happens. The city has not accepted our rule, and the resistance is expected to run {{turns}} more. The prefect has stopped promising an early end to it.

variants.headline: Resistance continues in an occupied city
body: In one of the occupied cities, the day's orders go up on the wall and come down before the ink dries. The city is expected to resist for {{turns}} more before the administration answers to us, according to the last dispatch.

variants.headline: {{population}} people in an occupied {{cityName}}
body: The map now shows {{cityName}} inside our borders, with {{population}} people counted in its streets. The map does not show that the city refuses us, and that it will resist for {{turns}} more. A conquest is easy to draw and hard to govern, and the men who drew it here have not explained how they mean to finish the job.

variants.headline: The old loyalty runs deep in {{cityName}}
body: At the market in {{cityName}}, a fishwife quoted her prices in {{formerOwner}}'s coin and took the money without a blush. Nobody reported her; half the queue was counting in the same currency. The city expects {{turns}} more of it. So does she.

variants.headline: Mood darkens in occupied {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} remains under occupation, and its own books put the mood of the streets at {{unrest}} on the happiness scale. Patrols have been doubled in the old quarter, and the prefect reports that {{turns}} more must pass before the city settles under our flag.

variants.headline: A new city: {{cityName}}
body: By nightfall on the first day, {{cityName}} had a fire, a well marked out and a name. Our settlers raised it under our flag, and the work ahead is the work every city begins with: houses, fields and walls.

variants.headline: A new city is founded
body: Our settlers have founded a new city, and its name has not yet reached the records. The stakes are driven, the ground is ours, and the building has begun.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{cityName}} is founded
body: Hear it, {{terms.civic.people}}! Our settlers have planted {{cityName}}, and the flag flies over a new city this morning! Learn the name and carry it down every street: {{cityName}}!

variants.headline: {{cityName}} begins its story
body: {{cityName}} begins life as a claim, a few families and a supply wagon that will not stay long. What the place becomes depends on what the nation sends next: seed, tools, soldiers or nothing. The cities we admire today all started with less, and none of them grew without help.

variants.headline: A new settlement at {{cityName}}
body: We are pleased to record the founding of {{cityName}}, settled under the nation's flag. The {{terms.civic.government}} has promised the town protection and a share of the next stores sent out. Settlers bound for the site may register at the capital for the road.

variants.headline: Who pays for the sign in {{cityName}}?
body: Madam, my son has gone out to {{cityName}} and asks me to paint its first sign. He says the town already calls itself the equal of any in the country, which is a fine thing to hear from a place with one street. Will you tell me who settles its accounts, so I send the bill to the right desk?

variants.headline: Settlers ready as {{town}} grows smaller
body: A party of settlers is ready to leave {{town}}, and the latest count shows the city smaller than before. In the lane by the gate, neighbors are asking who will go and who will take over the work they leave behind.

variants.headline: Settlers ready, spirits low in {{town}}
body: {{town}} has given part of its people to a settler party, and the city is smaller for it. Fewer mouths should mean fuller plates, yet the mood in the streets has soured. Nobody in charge has offered the city a reason.

variants.headline: Good cheer in {{town}} as settlers prepare to go
body: {{town}} is sending its settlers out, and the town is in good heart. The tables are less crowded and the news has lifted spirits. The council calls it proof that a city can give up a few households and still keep its people content.

variants.headline: One more thing to pack in {{town}}
body: The count in {{town}} is down by {{lost}}, and the carts at the end of Tanner's Row are loaded past the axles. A woman there is deciding which pots to take and which to give away. Her neighbor, who has agreed to keep the hens, has one condition: "Take the rooster."

variants.headline: {{city}} is eating into its stores
body: The granary keeper in {{city}} chalks the level on the doorpost every morning now. The city holds {{foodStored}} in store and loses {{shortfall}} of it each day. The chalk mark has not risen once this month.

variants.headline: Why {{city}} is starving in peacetime
body: No army stands outside {{city}}, and the city is going hungry anyway. It loses {{shortfall}} of food a day against a store of {{foodStored}}, and the loss is written plainly in the granary books. In wartime, hunger has an enemy to blame. In peace, it has a manager, and the manager has some explaining to do.

variants.headline: The granary at {{city}} is emptying
body: {{city}} has {{foodStored}} in the granary, and the level drops by {{shortfall}} every day. A baker on the high street has begun cutting loaves in half so that everyone in the queue gets something. She has stopped taking orders for the week ahead.

variants.headline: The food account of {{city}}
body: In the granary: {{foodStored}}.
Gone every day: {{shortfall}}.
Enemy at the gate: none. War: none. The books still end in hunger.

variants.headline: {{cityName}} is being razed
body: Smoke from {{cityName}} has been lying over the ridge road since dawn, and our soldiers are pulling the walls down stone by stone. {{turns}} more will finish it, and then the site will be bare.

variants.headline: A city is being razed
body: Our troops are burning a city that this paper cannot name. The reports give no name for it, only a site and a count: {{turns}} more of work.

variants.headline: The decision to raze {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} has {{turns}} left before it ceases to exist. When the last wall falls, the realm will have one less place to garrison, feed and govern, and one more stretch of open ground on its frontier. The order was ours, and so is whatever grows there next.

variants.headline: The end of {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}} will be gone in {{turns}}, and no stone of it will be left standing. It had its markets and its prayers, and both will end at the same hour. Let the gods it served remember the city, since the ground will not.

variants.headline: {{population}} people and {{turns}} left in {{cityName}}
body: {{population}} people remain in {{cityName}} while our fires eat through its streets. {{turns}} more will empty it, one way or another. The roads out of the city are the busiest streets it has left.
